title: Cheapest Path Down a Number Pyramid
statement:
A number pyramid pyramid has one number in its top row, two in the next, and so on: row i holds i + 1 numbers.

Start at the top and walk down one row at a time to the bottom row. From position j in a row you may step to position j or j + 1 in the row below (the two numbers right underneath it). Return the smallest possible sum of the numbers on such a path.

examples.why: 2 + 3 + 1 + 2. No other top-to-bottom path is cheaper.
Stepping to the smaller number each time takes the 2 and then has only 9s below it (sum 21). Taking the 3 first unlocks 1 + 1.
Adding the smallest number of each row gives 1, but the 1 and the bottom 0 are not connected. The real best path is 0 + 5 + 0.

constraints: row i has exactly i + 1 numbers
gen: (r, big) => { const n = big ? 200 : r.int(1, 7); const lo = big ? -10000 : -9, hi = big ? 10000 : 9; return [Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => r.arr(i + 1, lo, hi))]; }
hints: Greedy fails: a small number now can lead into an expensive corner. You need the best result over all continuations.
Define best(i, j) = cheapest sum from position j in row i down to the bottom. It only depends on the two positions under it.
Start from the bottom row and fold upward: each row becomes its own values plus the smaller of the two numbers below. One array of length n is enough.

explain.intuition:
From any spot, the cheapest way down is its own number plus the cheaper of the two spots right below it. That is a small recursion, and the same spot is shared by two parents, which is why trying every path repeats work: there are 2n−1 paths but only about n²/2 spots.

Work from the bottom up. The bottom row is already "cheapest from here". Each row above becomes value + min(below[j], below[j + 1]). When you reach the top row, its single number is the answer. Going bottom-up is nicer than top-down because the top has one cell, so there is no final "take the minimum of the last row" step and no edge cases at the borders.
steps: Copy the bottom row into an array best.
For each row i from the second-to-last up to the top, for each j from 0 to i: best[j] = pyramid[i][j] + min(best[j], best[j + 1]).
Reading left to right is safe: best[j + 1] still holds the row below when you use it.
pitfalls: Stepping to the smaller of the two numbers below. The second example shows it can walk into a dead end.
Summing the smallest number per row, ignoring that steps must connect (third example).
Allowing a step to j − 1. Only j and j + 1 are below position j.

solutions.title: Try every path
solutions.idea: Recurse from the top: each spot costs its value plus the cheaper of its two recursive results.

solutions.title: Top-down table
solutions.idea: Fill the cheapest sum to reach every spot from the top. Edge spots have one parent. The answer is the minimum of the last row.

solutions.title: Bottom-up in one array
solutions.idea: Fold the pyramid upward from the last row. Each spot keeps the cheapest sum from itself to the bottom.

followups: Return the path itself, as the list of numbers visited.
Allow a step to j − 1 as well. Does the bottom-up fold still work?
